source.title: GPT-2 Metadata Pretraining Towards Instruction Finetuning for Ukrainian

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some tables are flattened in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains GPT-2 models at several sizes and reports held-out language-model losses, but does not fit or evaluate scaling-law curves.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out loss and BrUK bits per character by model size. Its compute-optimal token estimates are used to guide training; they are not an experiment finding the loss-minimising parameter/token split. Results cited from Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a model-release paper for Ukrainian GPT-2. It uses Chinchilla Approach 2 estimates as a tool to pick training-token budgets (Table 1, Figure 1 shading) and reports its own models' losses. Its three runs (123M, 355M, 774M) differ in token count (6.29B to 21.4B), biases, initialisation, learning rate, optimiser (8-bit then 32-bit AdamW for Large) and hardware. No power law is fitted, no factor is isolated, and the span is under one order of magnitude. The falling losses therefore cannot bear on the power-law form or on any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors' main conclusion concerns releasing Ukrainian GPT-2 models trained on a single GPU (0.69 BPC baseline), metadata pretraining, and instruction-formatted POS/NER tasks. On size, they report lower losses for larger models, note that Large's low loss is due to a late-training spike, and see a narrow gap between Medium and Large. They suggest training Medium longer and say more data is needed to follow compute-optimal token predictions. They do not fit or claim a scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: This is a Ukrainian GPT-2 pretraining study, not a reproduction of the original scaling-law experiments; it trains three model sizes on UberText 2.0 and reports validation loss and BrUK bits per character.
record.method_sensitivity: Training token count and training details differ across the model sizes; the authors note that Large's validation loss is affected by a late-training spike.

fits_no_version.finding: Across three confounded runs (123M/355M/774M, with different tokens and recipes), held-out loss falls (2.38, 2.10, 1.82) and BrUK BPC falls (0.72, 0.70, 0.69). Table 2 title BLEURT rises (0.54, 0.57, 0.59) and tag IoU rises (0.47, 0.54, 0.56).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Uncontrolled size comparisons in a low-resource-language model release show monotone gains, but they are not a scaling-law test.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the Second Ukrainian Natural Language Processing Workshop (UNLP), Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Only three model sizes are reported, with differing training-token counts and implementation details. No power-law fits, uncertainty estimates, or controlled compute-optimal allocation comparison are reported. The authors identify a late-training spike affecting Large's validation loss.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 downstream metadata-prediction scores are not included as rows: the flattened text does not permit reliable assignment of all values to model and metric. This is why V6 is marked tested_not_extracted.

untested.parts: There is no power-law fit, no isolation of parameters, tokens or compute, and no span of several orders of magnitude.
Chinchilla estimates are only used to set token budgets. The loss-minimising allocation is not tested.
No comparison of shape at a fixed parameter count.
Not tested. Data are repeated (one epoch is 8202 updates), but no scaling law is fitted on repeated data.
Table 2 metadata scores rise with size, but the runs are confounded and no predictive relation is tested.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only in related work. The Chinchilla estimate is computed with nanoGPT's notebook and used to set budgets. The authors note that this estimate assumes no repeated tokens, which does not hold for their runs. Table 2 values appear assignable in order (BERTScore 0.90/0.91/0.91, mBART 0.94; BLEURT 0.54/0.57/0.59, mBART 0.74; IoU 0.47/0.54/0.56; Accuracy 0.64/0.71/0.71). They are not needed as rows because the study does not test V6. The reader's 'tests/T2' label and its V1 labels are withdrawn.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fit power laws or isolate parameters, tokens, and compute while holding the other factors fixed; does not test the claim over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run losses.
Compute-optimal token estimates are referenced for training decisions, but the study does not compare parameter/token allocations at fixed compute or test their growth with compute.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law test in another modality or training regime.

The paper reports downstream metadata-prediction metrics for models of different sizes, but the flattened Table 2 text does not allow the metric values to be assigned confidently to individual models and conditions.
No comparison of fit choices or exponents; the paper does not test whether a fitted scaling curve bends away from a power law.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small+
rows.operation_detail: Pretrained GPT-2 models at different sizes and reported held-out loss.
rows.note: The value is assigned to Small, Medium, and Large in table order; the paper says Large has a much lower validation loss and attributes it to a late-training spike.
rows.check: This is one model's held-out loss with no controlled comparison. It is a description of the model, not a scaling test. The value 2.38 is correctly assigned to Small+ (LSTM has no uk4b loss).

rows.subject: GPT-2 Medium+
rows.operation_detail: Pretrained GPT-2 models at different sizes and reported held-out loss.
rows.note: The paper suggests it might be beneficial to train Medium for longer.
rows.check: Medium+ was trained on fewer tokens (6.29B) than Small+ (6.87B), with the same recipe. The size effect is real but is only two points with no fit, so it cannot show a power law. The baseline being Small+ is fine.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Large
rows.operation_detail: Pretrained GPT-2 models at different sizes and reported held-out loss.
rows.note: The authors attribute Large's much lower validation loss to a spike toward the end of training.
rows.check: Large differs in tokens (21.4B vs 6.29B), biases, initialisation, learning rate and optimiser. The authors attribute its lower loss to a spike near the end of training, so the 1.82 is not a clean size effect.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small+
rows.operation_detail: Compared held-out BrUK bits per character across model sizes.
rows.note: The paper reports 28,643 test sentences in BrUK29k.
rows.check: This is a single-model BPC on BrUK29k with no controlled comparison.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Medium+
rows.operation_detail: Compared held-out BrUK bits per character across model sizes.
rows.note: The models were trained on different numbers of tokens.
rows.check: The BPC difference (0.72 to 0.70) is confounded by token count. It is two points with no fit.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Large
rows.operation_detail: Compared held-out BrUK bits per character across model sizes.
rows.note: The paper cautions that the models differ in training and implementation details.
rows.check: The change of 0.70 to 0.69 comes with roughly 3.4x more tokens and a different recipe. The authors note a narrow gap between Medium and Large. The change cannot be attributed to parameters.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
